unsaid.text: The explanatory statement says the measure would add a right to prior notification when medical services are offered to a child (except emergency treatment), remove the limit that crime notices apply only to events on school property during school hours, and require schools to notify parents if a child is removed from school without parental permission, including to stay at a youth shelter. Records would have to be produced within ten business days instead of the 45 days allowed by current law.

items.label: Initiative 638
items.title: Restrict girls’ school sports to students verified as female
items.mtype: Citizen-initiated state statute (initiative to the people)
items.ballot_title: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 concerns participation in athletics at K-12 schools. This measure would prohibit students it defines as “biologically male” from competing in certain school athletic activities intended for female students only. It would require verification of biological sex by students’ healthcare providers. Should this measure be enacted into law?
items.summary: Washington schools must offer sports without regard to sex but may provide separate teams based on sex, and state guidelines prohibit discrimination based on sex and gender identity. Initiative 638 would, in its own language, prohibit “biologically male students from competing with and against female students” on teams or in events designated for female students only. The Attorney General says this would generally prevent transgender girls from participating on girls’ teams, and would cover public K-12 schools and private schools that participate in the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association or similar organizations. Students in female-only categories would need a form signed by their personal health care provider verifying “biological sex.”
items.yes: A yes vote would prohibit students defined as biologically male from competing in school sports intended for female students only, and would require healthcare provider verification of biological sex for those students.
items.no: A no vote would leave current Washington law and state guidelines in place, which prohibit discrimination in school sports based on sex and gender identity while allowing separate teams based on sex.

fiscal.text: The Office of Financial Management’s fiscal impact statement says the initiative would not affect state or local revenue. It estimates the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction would incur a one-time cost of approximately $21,000 to update guidelines, and that local school districts would likely incur costs to revise policies and procedures, but that this impact is indeterminate.

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through August 31, 2026, Let’s Go Washington, the committee supporting Initiative 638, reported $8,059,297.89 in total contributions. Ballotpedia notes the committee is funding three initiatives on the ballot (Initiatives 1, 638 and 645), so that total covers all three. The three committees registered to oppose it (No Hate in WA State, Defend Washington and Permanent Defense PAC) reported $3,843,631.74 in total contributions, a figure Ballotpedia lists on the pages for all three initiatives.

for.text: The official argument for says “Female athletes deserve fair opportunities to build confidence, develop skills, and pursue goals,” and that the measure would affirm Title IX’s recognition of “the necessity of the female category.” The rebuttal says “A female athlete should not lose a starting position, medal, championship, or college recruiting opportunity because the category created for her was not protected.”

It says the verification would be modest: “during a private, consented visit, a licensed medical professional would verify sex based on the student’s birth records, medical history and/or a standard, non-invasive physical examination.” The rebuttal says “IL26-638 doesn’t require invasive or expensive exams.”

It says the measure would align Washington with other bodies: “Federal law, the Women’s Tennis Association, World Athletics, and the International Olympic Committee have all adopted policies to protect eligibility for the female category.” The rebuttal cites “at least 269 placements by male athletes competing in girls’ interscholastic categories, including 74 firsts and 156 top-three finishes.”

against.text: The official argument against says the measure “would require girls as young as 8 to undergo intrusive medical sex certification as a new part of sports physicals” and “bans parents from using birth certificates.” It says “These requirements apply to girls only, boys are exempt.”

It says the Washington State Nurses Association, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and doctors warn the measure would subject girls to “medically unnecessary, embarrassing, and potentially harmful genital exams.” It says “Today, students remain fully clothed during sports physicals,” and that many girls without a regular family doctor would be examined by “total strangers.”

It says “This statewide blanket ban to kick 5 - 10 trans girls off school teams will negatively impact all girls, leaving no room for case by case decisions,” and that coaches and athletes say “invasive genital exam requirements” would discourage girls from playing sports.

unsaid.label: What the verification would require, according to the Attorney General.
unsaid.text: The explanatory statement says verification “would have to be based on the student’s reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels,” and concludes: “Students would thus have to undergo some type of medical evaluation of their sex to participate in interschool sports designated for female students only.” The pamphlet arguments disagree about how invasive that evaluation would be.

items.label: Question 3
items.title: Replace party primaries with a single top-two primary
items.ballot_title: State Primary Elections. Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026?
items.summary: Question 3 would eliminate political party primaries for state elections. Instead there would be a single primary with all candidates, regardless of party, on one ballot; voters could vote for any candidate, and the two candidates with the most votes would advance to the general election. Candidates for governor and lieutenant governor would run and be listed jointly. Any group whose candidates for a statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary would get political party status. Ballotpedia notes the presidential primary would not be included, and that it is possible for two candidates of the same party to advance.
items.yes: A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election.
items.no: A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections.

fiscal.text: The state’s fiscal statement, written by the Executive Office of Administration and Finance, says the proposed law “has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 20, 2026, the committee supporting Question 3 (Coalition for Healthy Democracy 2026) reported $7,164,297.62 in total contributions, including $1,050,000.00 from David Randolph Peeler, its top listed donor. Two committees registered to oppose it (Voter Rights MA and Democratic Socialists Against Reactionary Rollbacks) reported $195,159.27 combined.

for.text: The official argument in favor was written by Danielle Allen of the Coalition for Healthy Democracy. It says “Many elections are over before most of us ever cast a ballot. Candidates can be blocked at party conventions. Today, two-thirds of the legislature is running unopposed.”

It argues that “All candidates appear on your primary ballot, and the top two advance to November where they need a majority of votes to win. Insiders have less control and we get fresh voices running for office.”
It concludes that “More competition means more accountability. Legislators who know voters can replace them listen to us and deliver real results.”

against.text: The official argument against was written by Vanessa A. Snow of Voter Rights MA. It says that “Similar top-two systems in California and Washington have favored wealthy, self-funded candidates who can out-advertise crowded fields and the corporate PACs seeking to purchase offices.”
It argues that “Third-party and independent candidates would be shut out of the general election, and working-class candidates would lose out on institutional support and access to party resources.”

It says the proposal “would limit voter choice by allowing only two candidates to advance to November” even if they belong to the same party, “reducing competition, lowering voter participation, worsening inequities, and narrowing debate.”

unsaid.label: Small parties could still win ballot status.
unsaid.text: The official summary says the law would give political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary. Neither argument mentions this provision.

unsaid.label: Where else top-two is used, and how ballots would look.
unsaid.text: Ballotpedia says that as of September 2025 California, Washington and Nebraska used a top-two primary for some elections. It says primary ballots under Question 3 would show the party or political designation from each candidate’s nomination papers, with the words “Endorsed by the political party or designation” added next to a candidate’s name at the request of both the candidate and the party.

items.label: Question 7
items.title: Allow single-family homes on lots of 5,000 square feet or more
items.ballot_title: Single Family Homes. Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026?
items.summary: Question 7 would allow single-family homes to be built in a residentially zoned area as long as the land is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet of land bordering the street, road or public way it faces, and has access to public sewer and water services. Cities and towns could reasonably regulate certain aspects of those homes, including height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking requirements and whether they can be rented out on a short-term basis. The Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities could issue guidance or regulations to administer the law.
items.yes: A YES VOTE would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more in residential areas, subject to reasonable local regulation of certain aspects of those homes.
items.no: A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to building single-family homes.

fiscal.text: The state’s fiscal statement, written by the Executive Office of Administration and Finance, says that if the law “enables the growth of housing in communities, it could provide positive new growth revenues to municipalities,” but that “it is difficult to project the potential scale of new growth.” It concludes the law has “no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 20, 2026, committees supporting Question 7 (Legalize Starter Homes, Abundant Housing Legalize Starter Homes and Democratic Socialists for a Fair Massachusetts) reported $1,757,560.37 in total contributions. Its top listed donors included the Greater Boston Real Estate Board and the Mass Association of Realtors PAC ($350,000.00 each). As of October 2026 no committees had registered in opposition.

for.text: The official argument in favor was written by Wesley Lima of Legalize Starter Homes. It says “Massachusetts is the hardest state in the country for young adults to buy a home. The middle class is shrinking because housing costs have doubled since 2014.”

It argues that “Requiring huge lot sizes to build a single-family home makes houses expensive, reduces construction of new single-family housing, and encourages developers to build giant McMansions to recoup land costs.”

It says a yes vote “would reduce minimum lot size requirements to 5,000 square feet - a size more typical of suburbs nationwide - in places with sufficient infrastructure, so we can have more affordable homes for young families and seniors.”

against.text: The official argument against was written by Adam Chapdelaine of the Massachusetts Municipal Association. It says the measure “would override local planning by requiring every city and town to allow single-family homes on lots as small as 5,000 square feet, regardless of existing neighborhoods, infrastructure or environmental conditions.”

It argues that “Local officials are directly responsible to taxpayers, and this would remove significant oversight on behalf of their residents.” Local officials “understand their communities best, and work with residents to plan for housing while balancing public safety, traffic, water and sewer capacity, schools, and environmental protection.”

It says the proposal “replaces thoughtful local planning with a one-size-fits-all mandate that ignores the individual needs of all 351 Massachusetts cities and towns,” and that communities should expand housing “through local planning and collaboration—not through a statewide mandate.”

unsaid.label: The measure has conditions and leaves some local rules in place.
unsaid.text: The official summary says a lot would need access to public sewer and water services, and that cities and towns could still reasonably regulate height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking and short-term rental of these homes. The pamphlet arguments do not address these provisions.

unsaid.label: Today’s minimum lot sizes are set locally and are often larger.
unsaid.text: Ballotpedia reports that minimum lot sizes are currently set by local governments, not state law. It quotes the state’s Comprehensive Housing Plan for 2025-2029: “Much of Massachusetts is covered by zoning districts that are quite simple: single-family homes with a minimum lot area of one-half to two acres.”

items.label: Proposition 41
items.title: Require audits of new special taxes and keep them under the spending limit
items.ballot_title: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
items.summary: Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exclude their revenues from the state spending limit approved by voters in 1979. For statewide special taxes, it would require a State Auditor review of the programs that would receive money from a voter-proposed special tax (after supporters gather 25 percent of the needed signatures), with a summary printed in the voter guide if the measure qualifies, and repeat audits every four years of programs funded by special taxes created after January 1, 2026. It also says other voter-approved measures on the same ballot are void if they conflict with it and it receives more yes votes.
items.yes: A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
items.no: A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

fiscal.text: The Legislative Analyst estimates an unknown net fiscal effect. State Auditor costs would increase, “in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time,” and would mostly be paid from the revenues of the new special taxes. Printing audit summaries in the voter guide could add “a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative.” There could be savings if the Auditor’s recommendations are implemented, but they “are not known.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 22, 2026, committees supporting Proposition 41 reported $68.8 million in contributions and committees opposing it (which also oppose Proposition 42 and support Proposition 40) reported $34.1 million. Ballotpedia lists Sergey Brin ($102,000,000.00), L. John Doerr III ($30,000,000.00) and Patrick Collison ($22,000,000.00) as top donors to the support committees, and notes those totals exceed the committees’ reported contributions because Building a Better California also funds other propositions.

for.text: The official argument in favor was signed by leaders of the California Society of CPAs and the California Taxpayers Association and by a former State Auditor. It says “Before we vote on new taxes to fund programs, voters should have access to independent information about how those programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding.”

It says “This year alone, California’s state government will spend more than $350 billion—a 79% increase in spending since 2019,” with “too little to show for it” from programs such as homelessness efforts, and that audits would help “identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse.”

It argues that “Prop. 41 doesn’t raise taxes—it protects taxpayers’ interests,” and that it “Requires all taxes to comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit—including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.”

against.text: The official argument against was written by Suzanne Jimenez of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West. It says “This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40,” and that “Prop. 41 isn’t about auditing new taxes. It’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid.”
It names Sergey Brin as “One of Prop. 41’s main funders” and says he has spent “over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 41 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax.”

Its rebuttal says Prop. 41 was “created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce,” would “cost the state time and money,” and that the Billionaire Tax is needed to fund healthcare, public education and food assistance.

unsaid.label: It could stop Proposition 40 from taking effect.
unsaid.text: The Legislative Analyst says that if Proposition 41 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, “then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters,” because courts could find the two conflict.

unsaid.label: Details of the audit rules.
unsaid.text: The audit would take place after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed, “which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot.” The Legislative Analyst says the audits would include “identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent,” and that the one-time cost of audits for special taxes that do not reach the ballot or are rejected would be paid from the state’s General Fund.

items.label: Proposition 42
items.title: Ban new state taxes on personal property and savings, and limit retroactive taxes
items.ballot_title: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
items.summary: Proposition 42 would amend the California Constitution to prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property, including assets in retirement and investment accounts, and new state taxes that apply retroactively to things that happened in the past. It would apply to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026. Ballotpedia notes an exception for taxes enacted by the Legislature after the Governor declares a physical-threat or fiscal emergency, with revenue limited to addressing the emergency. It also says other voter-approved measures on the same ballot are void if they conflict with it and it receives more yes votes.
items.yes: A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
items.no: A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

fiscal.text: The Legislative Analyst’s estimate is a “Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.” It says the measure “restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future,” and that “When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 22, 2026, committees supporting Proposition 42 reported $138.4 million in contributions and committees opposing it (which also oppose Proposition 41) reported $34.1 million. Ballotpedia lists Sergey Brin ($102,000,000.00), L. John Doerr III ($30,000,000.00) and Patrick Collison ($22,000,000.00) as top donors to the support committees, and notes those totals exceed the committees’ reported contributions because Building a Better California also funds other propositions.

for.text: The official argument in favor was signed by leaders of the California Small Business Association, AMVETS Department of California and the California Senior Alliance. It says “California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it.”

It says the measure “Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts,” and notes that “the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts” in recent years.

It argues “The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past.” The rebuttal asks “should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?”

against.text: The official argument against was written by Suzanne Jimenez of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West. It says “This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40,” and that “Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid.”

It says the initiative “was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce,” and that Sergey Brin, one of its main funders, has spent “over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax.”

Its rebuttal says the California Billionaires Tax “ONLY applies to billionaires” and calls Prop. 42 “a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes.”

unsaid.label: It could stop Proposition 40 from taking effect.
unsaid.text: The Legislative Analyst says that if Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, “then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters,” because courts could find the two conflict.

unsaid.label: Today’s personal property taxes and financial assets.
unsaid.text: The Legislative Analyst says the state and local governments already tax some personal property, such as the vehicle license fee and property taxes on business equipment. It says that while the state taxes income from financial assets, “there is no tax for simply owning those assets.”

items.label: Proposition 136
items.title: Set a 4.4% limit on the state income tax rate
items.ballot_title: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes capping the state income tax rate at 4.4% of federal taxable income for individuals and corporations?
items.summary: Proposition 136 would set a 4.4 percent limit in state law on the income tax rate for individual and corporate taxpayers, beginning January 1, 2027. It would not change today’s 4.4 percent rate. It would not change the process for adjusting the rate: the Legislature or a citizen initiative may still reduce it, and the Colorado Constitution already requires voter approval of tax rate increases. Because it is a statute, Ballotpedia notes, the Legislature could amend or repeal it. The Blue Book says that if Proposition 136 and Amendment 87 (a graduated income tax) both pass, “the exact outcome is unclear.”
items.yes: A yes vote on Proposition 136 establishes the current state income tax rate of 4.4 percent as the maximum rate.
items.no: A no vote on Proposition 136 keeps the current state income tax rate of 4.4 percent without establishing a new limit in statute.

fiscal.text: The Blue Book says the measure “results in no change to state or local government revenue or spending. For this reason, the measure has no fiscal impact.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 14, 2026, committees supporting Proposition 136 (Brighter Colorado and Keep Colorado Affordable) reported $3,878,275.00 in total contributions, with top listed donors Common Sense America ($2,000,000.00) and the GOPAC Election Fund ($1,000,000.00). Committees opposing it reported $3,359,500.43.

for.text: The Blue Book argument for says “Proposition 136 reinforces voter support for maintaining the current state income tax rate. The current rate, overwhelmingly approved by voters in 2022, is fair and keeps Colorado’s tax rate among the lowest in the country.”
The Independence Institute says “Colorado’s flat 4.4% tax rate remains competitive regionally, as it is lower than the flat and top rates of Utah, New Mexico, Idaho and Montana.”

Michael Fields, executive director of Advance Colorado, says the measure is “a clear counter to the far left’s attempt to hike taxes in Colorado, price people out of the state we love, and drive business out. We’ll always fight to protect TABOR and keep our taxes low.”

against.text: The Blue Book argument against says “This initiative is designed to put Amendment 87 into legal jeopardy, causing confusion and a potentially costly legal battle to resolve. After the 2026 election, Proposition 136 has no effect, since raising tax rates already requires voter approval and any future approval would override this measure.”

The Bell Policy Center says “This measure is only meaningful because it conflicts with the graduated income tax that is proposed in Amendment 87. The tax rate is already 4.4 percent and the constitution states that only a vote of the people can increase tax rates.”
New Era Colorado says “Giant corporations and the wealthy should not pay the same income tax rate as people earning $50,000 a year.”

unsaid.label: What happens if both this measure and Amendment 87 pass.
unsaid.text: The Blue Book says that if both pass, the Amendment 87 rate for incomes over $500,000 “would be higher than the 4.4 percent limit in Proposition 136,” and that “Generally, when parts of voter-approved measures conflict, the policy outcome is determined by the measure that receives more votes. However, if both measures are approved by voters, the exact outcome is unclear.” It says the Legislature or a court would resolve any conflict. See our page on Amendment 87.

items.label: Proposition 144
items.title: Require ID to vote in every election, including by mail
items.ballot_title: Proposed amendment to the Constitution by the Legislature relating to election requirements. Amending Article VII, Constitution of Arizona, by adding Section 19. Requires all voters, including voters who vote by mail, to show government-issued ID to vote in each election; makes other changes to election administration and campaign finance prohibitions.
items.summary: Proposition 144, called the Fast Accurate Secure Transparent Election Results Act, would amend the Arizona Constitution to reaffirm that only U.S. citizens may register and vote; require voters to present valid government-issued proof of identity before casting a ballot, whether voting in person or by another method, as prescribed by law; require that voters be given the option to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on Election Day; prohibit foreign nationals from contributing or spending money to influence an Arizona election; allow the people and the Legislature to enact election laws, including on early and mail voting, if they are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest; and require the Legislature to fund implementation. It would apply to elections on or after January 1, 2028.
items.yes: A yes vote shall have the effect of amending the Arizona Constitution to: (1) require voters to show proof of identity when voting in each election, including when voting by mail; (2) changing existing proof of identity requirements to limit acceptable documentation to government-issued ID; (3) require election officials to provide all voters the option to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on election day; (4) prohibit foreign nationals from contributing or spending to influence elections in Arizona and prohibit anyone from knowingly accepting such contributions, similar to prohibitions that already exist in federal law; (5) create a new standard for judicial review of election laws under the Arizona Constitution, which may make it harder to challenge election laws; and (6) require the legislature to appropriate money necessary to implement these provisions.
items.no: A no vote shall have the effect of maintaining current constitutional provisions governing elections.

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 24, 2026, no committee had registered to support Proposition 144. Two committees registered in opposition, Protect the Vote Arizona and Will of the People, reported $1,276,143.13 in total contributions. Ballotpedia notes that Arizona Free Enterprise Club ($9,639.65) and Freedom Club PAC ($17,937) made independent expenditures supporting it.

for.text: Rep. Alexander Kolodin, the measure’s sponsor, writes in the pamphlet: “A YES vote guarantees four things. Only United States citizens may vote in Arizona elections — period. Every voter provides a government-issued ID, so we know each ballot is cast by the person casting it.”
He argues that “Election Day means Election Day, and you’ll have fast results you can trust on election night,” and that “Arizona has been a national punchline for slow counts and broken trust.”

Heritage Action for America says “A loophole exists in Arizona law that allows foreign nationals to fund ballot measures in our state,” and another supporter says the measure puts four protections into the constitution “where they can’t be repealed by a legislative majority.”

against.text: The Arizona Public Health Association says “Arizona already has a secure vote-by-mail system. Voters must sign their ballot envelopes. Election workers compare those signatures with the voter’s record,” and that Proposition 144 “will make it much harder to vote early or by mail for no reason.”

Vitalyst Health Foundation says “Proposition 144 eliminates current identification options such as a utility bill, bank statement, or insurance card,” and that “Both Democratic and Republican election officials oppose Proposition 144 because it imposes unrealistic mandates on already under-resourced local election offices.”

The League of Women Voters of Arizona says “Constitutional amendments should protect fundamental rights, not lock election administration policies into place,” and that the measure places “detailed election procedures beyond the reach of ordinary legislative review and improvement.”

unsaid.label: It would change how courts review election laws.
unsaid.text: The ballot language says the measure would “create a new standard for judicial review of election laws under the Arizona Constitution, which may make it harder to challenge election laws.” The Legislative Council analysis describes it as allowing the people and the Legislature to enact election laws, including on early and mail voting, if they are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest.

unsaid.label: What Arizona requires today.
unsaid.text: Ballotpedia reports that Arizona currently requires voters to present photo identification or two forms of non-photo identification when voting in person, that the requirement is in state statute rather than the Constitution, and that there is no voter ID requirement for absentee or mail-in voting.

fiscal.text: Arizona law requires the Joint Legislative Budget Committee (JLBC) staff to summarize the fiscal impact of each voter initiative, and the JLBC states that “This requirement excludes legislatively referred propositions.” This measure was referred by the legislature, so the official pamphlet has no JLBC fiscal summary for it. The Legislative Council analysis in the pamphlet does not include a cost estimate, and we did not find another official one. The measure itself would require the legislature to appropriate any money necessary to implement it.

items.label: Proposition 318
items.title: Restrict girls’ sports and school private spaces by sex recorded at birth
items.ballot_title: Referred to the people by the Legislature relating to student athletics. Amending Section 15-120.02, Arizona Revised Statutes. Requires all schools and athletic associations to designate athletic teams as male, female, or coed based on the biological sex of the athletes as defined at birth; prohibits these entities from authorizing use of private spaces not designated for a person’s sex.
items.summary: Proposition 318, the Protect Girls’ Sports in Arizona Act, would require public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor teams to designate each as male, female or coed based on athletes’ biological sex, and would prohibit males from playing on female-designated teams. Sex would be defined as recorded at birth on the original birth certificate. It would also prohibit schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations from authorizing anyone to use restrooms, locker rooms, shower rooms or other private spaces not designated for that person’s biological sex, and would expand who may sue and be sued for violations. Ballotpedia says current Arizona law applies only to public schools and private schools that compete against them.
items.yes: A yes vote shall have the effect of: (1) requiring private schools, public schools, and athletic associations to designate every athletic team as male, female, or coed/mixed based on sex and to prevent males from joining female teams; existing law imposes this requirement only on public schools and those competing against them; (2) prohibiting schools and athletic associations from authorizing anyone to use private spaces (such as restrooms) not designated for that individual’s sex; (3) defining sex as an individual’s biological status as male or female as recorded at birth on an original birth certificate; and (4) authorizing athletes to sue schools and athletic associations that knowingly violate this law.
items.no: A no vote shall have the effect of maintaining the current laws relating to student athletics.

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 24, 2026, the committee supporting Proposition 318, Protect Girls’ Sports in AZ, reported $3,600.00 in total contributions. The committee opposing it, Will of the People, reported $871,000.00 and is also registered against Propositions 142, 144 and 320.

for.text: Attorney Thomas Bouman writes in the pamphlet that “girls’ sports should be reserved for girls,” and that when biological males compete in female divisions, “the physical advantages of male physiology—greater muscle mass, bone density, and speed—can displace female athletes from podiums, scholarships, and roster spots.”
He says the measure “also protects privacy” in locker rooms and showers, and that it is narrowly drawn: “It does not create criminal penalties. It does not regulate private youth sports.”

A collegiate volleyball player and coach writes that “boys who identify a certain way should not be allowed to bypass the common-sense rules that protect women and girls,” and that girls’ ability to compete on girls’ teams should not depend on politics.

against.text: The League of Women Voters of Arizona says the measure “addresses a situation that affects very few students, yet it imposes statewide mandates on every public school, many private schools, colleges, universities, and athletic associations,” and “invites costly litigation by creating new private rights of action.”

State Sen. Mitzi Epstein says “Prop 318 would subject girls to invasive inspections and questions about their gender,” and that it “create[s] new ways to start lawsuits” accusing any girl of not being feminine enough. She says it would betray Title IX’s promise to women and girls.

The League adds that decisions about student well-being “should be guided by educators, parents, and established athletic policies—not broad mandates written into law through a statewide ballot measure.” Other opponents say local schools and sports associations, not politicians, should handle the issue.

unsaid.label: The measure covers restrooms and locker rooms, not only sports.
unsaid.text: The Legislative Council analysis says Proposition 318 would also prohibit public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that maintain private spaces integral to athletic engagement from authorizing anyone to use a private space not designated for that person’s biological sex as recorded at birth on their original birth certificate.

unsaid.label: Changes would be hard to make later.
unsaid.text: The pamphlet notes that under Proposition 105 (1998), measures like this one “cannot be changed in the future if approved on the ballot except by a three-fourths vote of the members of each house of the legislature and if the change furthers the purpose of the original ballot measure, by an initiative petition or by referring the change to the ballot.”

fiscal.text: Arizona law requires the Joint Legislative Budget Committee (JLBC) staff to summarize the fiscal impact of each voter initiative, and the JLBC states that “This requirement excludes legislatively referred propositions.” This measure was referred by the legislature, so the official pamphlet has no JLBC fiscal summary for it. The Legislative Council analysis in the pamphlet does not include a cost estimate, and we did not find another official one.

items.label: Amendment 3
items.title: Raise the homestead exemption and cap non-homestead assessment increases at 5%
items.ballot_title: Increased homestead exemption; lower cap on increases in non-homestead property assessments.
items.summary: Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, adjusted for inflation after that. People who were not Florida residents on December 31, 2026 would get the existing exemption when they first qualify, with the larger exemption starting in the fifth year. It would lower the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead property, such as rentals and commercial property, from 10% to 5%. It would require the Legislature to set a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities to raise the exemption up to full assessed value, and would limit what counties and municipalities may spend property taxes on to listed purposes. It takes effect January 1, 2027.
items.yes: A yes vote would approve the amendment: the non-school homestead exemption would rise to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, the annual cap on non-homestead assessment increases would drop from 10% to 5%, and counties and municipalities would be limited to listed purposes when spending property taxes.
items.no: A no vote would leave the current homestead exemption, the 10% cap on non-homestead assessment increases, and current rules on local property tax spending in place.

fiscal.text: The Florida Revenue Estimating Conference’s middle estimate (reviewed June 12 and July 10, 2026) is a reduction in local non-school property tax revenue of $4,929.5 million in 2027-28 and $8,714.5 million in 2028-29, rising to a recurring reduction of $11,834.7 million per year. It estimates no impact on school taxes. It says the effect of requiring the Legislature to set procedures for fully exempting homesteads from county and municipal levies is unknown, because it depends on future legislative action. The campaigns make their own claims, which are not official estimates. The Vote No campaign says the amendment “could eventually bleed $34 billion from local government budgets.” The Vote Yes campaign says it will “help a majority of Florida homeowners achieve SIGNIFICANT savings on their future property tax bills.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 9, 2026, the committee supporting Amendment 3 (Vote Yes on 3) reported $21,516,510.33 in total contributions, including $19,500,000.00 from Florida Realtors. Committees opposing it reported $1,618,801.49 combined.

for.text: Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) says “Property tax revenue collected by local governments has nearly doubled in the past seven years and is expected to reach an astounding $83 billion by 2032. Florida homeowners need relief. Now is the time to stand up for taxpayers, enact a historic reform, and save the home of every Floridian.”

State Sen. Bryan Avila (R) says the amendment “takes a historic step, providing meaningful relief for Florida families, while protecting businesses from extreme tax increases and safeguarding local funding for education, law enforcement, infrastructure, and other essential government functions.”

The Republican Party of Florida says “Homeowners shouldn’t be taxed out of the homes they’ve worked for. Amendment 3 delivers real tax relief, slows runaway assessments, and makes local governments spend your money on core priorities.” Sen. Rick Scott (R) says “every county has waste to cut.”

against.text: Sadaf Knight of the Florida Policy Institute says the measure “does not represent cost savings, but rather a cost shift — one that will force local lawmakers to cut local services that families rely upon or increase other taxes and fees to make up for the missing revenue.”

Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan (D) says the reduction “will inevitably result in roads deteriorating, libraries, pools, and parks closing, public safety response times going up, housing affordability worsening, and more homeless on our streets.”

Former state Sen. Jeff Brandes, president of the Florida Policy Project, says “Nobody in all of Florida understands how this is going to play out. We have no models, no math, nothing. It’s budget chaos.” Former county commissioner Bryan Desolge says the bills for “public safety, roads and bridges, stormwater protection and even hurricane response don’t go away.”

unsaid.label: A court found the original ballot language defective.
unsaid.text: Ballotpedia reports that on August 3, 2026, a Leon County circuit judge ruled that the Legislature’s title and summary were “clearly and conclusively defective,” kept that language off the ballot, and ordered the Attorney General to submit corrected language within 10 days. The title and summary on this page come from the state’s booklet updated September 3, 2026.

unsaid.label: How far the exemption could go, and who gets the smaller one.
unsaid.text: The Revenue Estimating Conference says the amendment would require the Legislature to prescribe a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities to raise the exemption so that all homesteads are fully exempt from county and municipal levies, and that “No timeline or limit is provided.” People who did not maintain a permanent residence in Florida as of December 31, 2026 would receive a $50,000 exemption for four years and the larger exemption in the fifth year.

items.label: Question 4
items.title: Allow voters to register on Election Day
items.ballot_title: Election Day Registration. Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026?
items.summary: Question 4 would let eligible people register to vote, or update their registration address, on Election Day. They would go to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours, present proof of residency and sign a written oath certifying that they are a U.S. citizen, at least 18, not legally prohibited from voting, and have not voted and will not vote in the same election elsewhere. Providing false information would be a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison or a fine of up to $10,000. Someone without proof of residency could cast a provisional ballot. People already registered could not change party affiliation on Election Day. It would take effect January 1, 2028.
items.yes: A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day.
items.no: A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration.

fiscal.text: The state’s fiscal statement, written by the Executive Office of Administration and Finance, says the proposed law “has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 20, 2026, committees supporting Question 4 reported $329,753.70 in total contributions. As of October 2026 no committees had registered in opposition.

for.text: The official argument in favor was written by Norma B. Shulman of YES on Election Day Registration. It says “This law would give eligible Massachusetts citizens the ability to register or update their address on Election Day – an opportunity voters in the rest of New England already have.”

It argues that “Allowing voters to register at the polls will give thousands of citizens the chance to participate in important national elections. This policy especially helps those who move frequently, like young people and renters.”

It says the law is secure: “Election Day registrants must present verified proof of residence at the polls and sign an oath backed by severe felony penalties to ensure accountability and deter fraud. Provisional ballots would be available to protect the integrity of the vote if documentation is missing.”

against.text: The official argument against was written by Amy Carnevale of the Massachusetts Republican Party. It says same-day registration eliminates “the advance period during which election officials can examine a registrant’s identity, residence, eligibility, or duplicate registration before a ballot is issued.”

It argues that officials “would be required to make those determinations at the polling place, under substantial time pressure and amid the extraordinary demands of Election Day,” and that errors “may not be discovered until after the ballot has been cast and commingled with all others, when it can no longer be identified or withdrawn.”

It concludes that the question “would replace advance review with hurried, same-day judgments that could create avoidable vulnerabilities in election administration, increase the risk that unlawful ballots could affect close contests, and weaken confidence that every ballot was lawfully cast.”

unsaid.label: What happens to a provisional ballot.
unsaid.text: Under the official summary, a provisional ballot cast without proof of residency would be counted only if the person returned with the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election, within two days after a state primary, or within six days after a state election.

unsaid.label: Today’s deadline and early-voting exception.
unsaid.text: Ballotpedia reports that Massachusetts voters currently must register 10 days before an election, but because early voting begins 17 days before the election, some people who vote early can register on the same day they cast their ballot. It says 21 states and the District of Columbia offer same-day registration on Election Day.

items.label: Question 9
items.title: Keep or repeal the 2024 firearms law
items.ballot_title: Firearms Regulation. Do you approve of a law summarized below, which was approved by the House of Representatives on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 124 to 33, and approved by the Senate on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 35 to 5?
items.summary: Question 9 is a referendum on a 2024 law (Chapter 135, also called An Act Modernizing Firearm Laws) that made many changes to Massachusetts firearms law. According to the Attorney General’s summary, it lets school administrators and licensed healthcare providers ask a court for an Extreme Risk Protection Order; imposes penalties for possessing, making or transferring untraceable “ghost guns” and requires serial numbers on firearms other than antiques and relics; requires people to be 21 to own semiautomatic rifles or shotguns; expands the definitions of “machine gun” and “silencer”; bars carrying firearms in government buildings, polling locations and schools, with exceptions; and creates a public data dashboard. A yes vote keeps the law; a no vote repeals it.
items.yes: A YES VOTE would keep in place the law, which increases the regulation of firearms, including ghost guns, machine guns, and assault-style weapons.
items.no: A NO VOTE would repeal this law.

fiscal.text: The state’s fiscal statement, written by the Executive Office of Administration and Finance, says that since the law passed in 2024 “the Commonwealth has made significant investments to implement the law including training employees, promulgating new gun licensure processes, and developing IT infrastructure,” and that “Repealing the law would require the Commonwealth to expend resources in suspending or re-directing those investments.”

money.text: In reports Ballotpedia had processed through October 20, 2026, committees supporting a yes vote (Yes for A Safe Massachusetts and Democratic Socialists for a Fair Massachusetts) reported $896,930.04 in total contributions, with the Massachusetts Teachers Association the top listed donor ($500,237.00). The committee supporting a no vote, The Civil Rights Coalition, reported $593,467.57.

for.text: The official argument for a yes vote was written by Ned Notis-McConarty of Vote Yes for a Safe Massachusetts. It says the law made “vital updates, including banning ghost guns; outlawing devices that turn semi-automatic weapons into machine guns; expanding tools to help prevent firearm suicide and mass shootings; creating a firearms data dashboard to better understand gun trafficking.”

It argues that “Massachusetts has a gun death rate 70% lower than the national average,” and that “Critical elements of the 2024 law are actively being implemented; they are already helping keep our communities safe.”

It concludes that a yes vote “will preserve this law, safeguard important progress, and allow us to continue the work of eradicating gun violence. Repealing it would make everyone in Massachusetts less safe.”

against.text: The official argument for a no vote was written by Toby Leary of The Civil Rights Coalition. It says “Before the new law, the state already had some of the strictest gun laws in the country,” and calls Chapter 135 “a deeply flawed, 116-page piece of bureaucratic overreach that wastes valuable tax dollars and burdens local communities.”

It argues the law “mandates an expensive, real-time electronic tracking system that the state hasn’t funded and doesn’t know how to build,” and “forces local police departments to enforce a confusing patchwork of vague rules, pulling officers away from investigating violent crime.”

It says state agencies issued “dozens of clarifications for rules that treat harmless historical re-enactors and antique hobbyists like criminals,” and urges voters to demand “common-sense, transparent legislation focused on violent criminals, not limiting citizens’ civil rights.”

unsaid.label: The law’s firearm registration system.
unsaid.text: Ballotpedia reports that the law requires the Department of Criminal Justice Information Services to develop and maintain a real-time electronic system for firearm registration, and requires a basic firearms safety certificate to apply for a Firearm Identification Card or License to Carry. The Attorney General’s summary in the voter guide does not mention these provisions; the argument against refers to the tracking system.

unsaid.label: What the summary says about assault-style weapons already owned.
unsaid.text: The official summary says the law “clarifies how to determine whether a firearm is an assault-style weapon and the circumstances under which a person may continue to possess assault-style weapons and large capacity feeding devices they already own.” Neither argument describes this part of the law.
